caption:
Lisbon left a whole church without a roof on purpose — and once locked prisoners in cells that flooded with every high tide. 👀

Comment which one shocked you most 👇

facts.headline: Political prisoners were once held in cells that flooded at high tide
facts.body_html: Belém Tower's lower chambers were built for cannon storage, but from the 1580s to the 1830s they doubled as a state prison for political opponents — cells sitting below the waterline, where inmates reportedly stood in water up to their waists whenever the tide came in.

Torre de Belem Lisbon close up turret

facts.headline: A tax on pepper and cinnamon paid for this monastery
facts.body_html: King Manuel I funded Jerónimos Monastery with a 5% tax on every spice shipment sailing home from Vasco da Gama's India route — roughly 70kg of gold a year, in thanks for the voyage that first opened it.

facts.headline: This earthquake hit while the whole city was in church
facts.body_html: On All Saints' Day, 1755, three tremors in ten minutes leveled most of Lisbon while congregations packed the churches for morning Mass — the quake, tsunami, and fires that followed killed an estimated 30,000-40,000 people.
suggested_queries: Baixa Lisbon downtown grid streets aerial

facts.headline: This church has had no roof for over 270 years — on purpose
facts.body_html: Carmo Convent's stone nave collapsed in the 1755 earthquake and was deliberately never rebuilt, left open to the sky as a permanent memorial — you can still walk through its Gothic arches with nothing but clouds overhead.
suggested_queries: Carmo Convent ruins Lisbon roofless nave
Convento do Carmo Lisbon Gothic arches sky

facts.headline: An Eiffel protégé built this iron elevator in the middle of downtown
facts.body_html: The Santa Justa Lift, opened in 1902, was designed by Raoul Mesnier du Ponsard, a student of Gustave Eiffel himself — its neo-Gothic ironwork still hauls riders between Lisbon's lower and upper old town today.
suggested_queries: Santa Justa Lift Lisbon elevator street view
Elevador de Santa Justa Lisbon top platform

facts.headline: This bridge only got its current name after a revolution
facts.body_html: Built by the same American company behind San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge, this Tagus River crossing opened in 1966 as Salazar Bridge, named for Portugal's dictator — it was renamed 25 de Abril after the 1974 revolution that overthrew him.
suggested_queries: 25 de Abril Bridge Lisbon Tagus river
Ponte 25 de Abril Lisbon suspension towers

facts.headline: A cardinal's 1934 trip to Rio is why this statue exists
facts.body_html: After seeing Rio's Christ the Redeemer in 1934, Lisbon's cardinal pushed to build a Portuguese version as thanks for the country being spared from World War II — Cristo Rei finally opened in 1959, standing 110 meters tall above the river.
